MEC2047S · Dynamics I · Part I: Kinematics (L01–L17)

Dynamics, gently.

A plain-language companion to your lecture notes. It explains what each formula means, why it has the shape it has, and how to draw velocity and acceleration diagrams that earn full marks.

Kinematics is the geometry of motion. It asks where things are, how fast they move and how that speed changes, and it never asks why. Forces come later, in Part II. Everything in this half of the course comes from one chain of ideas:

\[ \text{position} \;\xrightarrow{\;d/dt\;}\; \text{velocity} \;\xrightarrow{\;d/dt\;}\; \text{acceleration} \]

Integration walks the chain backwards. The rest of the course is about two choices: which coordinates to describe the motion in, and which reference point to measure it from. Once you see each topic as one of those two choices, the whole course hangs together.

The colour code in every diagram

  • Blue: an absolute vector you already know completely, such as the velocity of a pin on a driven crank.
  • Amber: a normal component, \(\omega^2 r\). Once the velocities are solved, this is always fully known.
  • Green: a vector perpendicular to a bar. You know its direction but not its size until the diagram closes.
  • Crimson: the absolute vector you are solving for, such as the speed of a slider.
  • Grey dashes: construction lines. They show a direction before you know where the vector ends.

How to use this book

  • Read with your lecture slides open. Each chapter names the lectures it covers, and most worked examples are the same ones from your slides, slowed right down.
  • Look for the green “Why” boxes. They explain the science behind a formula, so you can rebuild it in the exam if your memory fails.
  • Use the step-through diagrams. Click Next step (or tap a numbered step) to watch a velocity or acceleration diagram being built one line at a time, in the order you would draw it on paper.
  • Chapters 9 and 10 are the heart of the book. If you only have one evening, read those two and Chapter 11.

Why the diagrams matter so much

Look at the review lectures. The 2016, 2021 and 2022 exam questions all ask you to draw a relative velocity or acceleration vector diagram “to the scale given” and then measure an answer from it. In the 2022 memo, part (b), the acceleration diagram alone, is worth 9 marks. Ticks go to each vector’s magnitude and direction, to the angles, to “all arrows” and to “diagram correct”. This is a drawing skill as much as a maths skill, and it can be learned like a recipe. Chapters 9 and 10 give you that recipe.

Chapter 1 · Lecture L01

The toolkit you will use every day

In this chapter
  • Vectors, and how the course writes them
  • The two triangle rules that solve most vector diagrams
  • The one cross product you need, \(\omega\hat k\times\vec r\)
  • Slope, area and the chain rule

L01 is a checklist of maths you are expected to already have. This chapter keeps only the parts that will come up again and again in kinematics, and says where each one gets used.

Scalars and vectors

A scalar has only a size: time, mass, distance travelled, speed. A vector has a size and a direction: position, displacement, velocity, acceleration, force. In this course a vector is written with an arrow, \(\vec v\), and its size (the magnitude) is written without one, \(v\) or \(|\vec v|\).

You will meet two ways of writing the same vector:

\[ \vec v = \underbrace{(5.32\ \text{m/s},\ \measuredangle -117^\circ)}_{\text{magnitude, angle}} \qquad\text{or}\qquad \vec v = \underbrace{-2.44\,\hat i + 4.73\,\hat j\ \ \text{m/s}}_{\text{components}} \]

The angle form is the one your memos use for final answers. Angles are measured from the positive \(x\)-axis, anticlockwise positive. Converting between them is the bread and butter of the course:

\[ v_x = v\cos\theta,\quad v_y = v\sin\theta \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad v=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2},\quad \theta=\tan^{-1}\!\frac{v_y}{v_x}\ \text{(check the quadrant!)} \]
Common slip

Your calculator’s \(\tan^{-1}\) only returns angles between −90° and +90°. A vector like \(-2.44\hat i + 4.73\hat j\) points up and to the left, so its angle is \(180^\circ - 62.7^\circ = 117.3^\circ\), not 62.7°. Sketch the vector before trusting the button.

The two triangle rules

Almost every vector diagram in this course is a triangle. You can measure it with a ruler, or solve it exactly with one of these two rules.

\[ \textbf{Sine rule:}\ \ \frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C} \qquad\qquad \textbf{Cosine rule:}\ \ a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A \]
Which one, when?

Use the cosine rule when you know two sides and the angle between them. That is the typical relative velocity case: you know \(v_A\), \(v_B\) and the angle between their directions, and you want \(v_{B/A}\).

Use the sine rule when you know all three directions (so all three angles) and one side. That is the typical rigid-body case: one velocity is known completely and the other two are known only by direction. Most of Chapter 9 runs on the sine rule.

The one cross product you need

For flat (planar) motion, every angular velocity points along \(\hat k\), straight out of the page. Anticlockwise (CCW) is positive. The cross product with a position vector then has a very simple meaning:

\[ \omega\hat k \times (x\,\hat i + y\,\hat j) \;=\; \omega\,(-y\,\hat i + x\,\hat j) \]
Why this works

Look at the result: the vector \((x, y)\) has become \((-y, x)\). That is the same vector turned 90° anticlockwise, then stretched by \(\omega\). So “\(\vec\omega\times\vec r\)” just means turn \(\vec r\) a quarter-turn in the direction of spin, and scale it by \(\omega\). That is why the velocity of a point on a spinning body is always perpendicular to the line from the centre, and why its size is \(\omega r\). You will use this idea in Chapters 6, 9 and 10.

The handy unit-vector results are \(\hat k\times\hat i = \hat j\) and \(\hat k\times\hat j = -\hat i\).

Calculus as pictures

  • A derivative is a slope. \(v = ds/dt\) is the slope of the position–time graph.
  • An integral is an area. \(\Delta s = \int v\,dt\) is the area under the velocity–time graph.
  • The chain rule turns geometry into velocity. If \(x = 0.2\cos\theta\) and \(\theta\) changes with time, then \(\dot x = -0.2\sin\theta\,\dot\theta\). That one line is the whole idea of Chapter 7.

Dots mean time derivatives: \(\dot\theta = d\theta/dt = \omega\) and \(\ddot\theta = d^2\theta/dt^2 = \alpha\).

Units and significant figures

  • Angles in kinematics formulas are in radians. Convert revolutions per minute with \(\omega = N\cdot\frac{2\pi}{60}\). For example, 1500 rev/min = 157 rad/s.
  • Tutorials ask for 3 significant figures. Keep 4 or more in your working and round only at the end.
  • Check units at the end of every answer. \(\omega^2 r\) is (rad/s)²·m = m/s², and \(\omega r\) is m/s.
In one breath
  • Vectors carry a size and a direction. Sketch before using \(\tan^{-1}\).
  • Cosine rule: two sides and the angle between them. Sine rule: one side and all the angles.
  • \(\omega\hat k\times\vec r\) means turn \(\vec r\) 90° the way it spins and multiply by \(\omega\).
  • Derivative = slope, integral = area, chain rule = geometry into velocity.
Chapter 2 · Lectures L02–L03

Straight-line motion

In this chapter
  • The three defining equations, and where the third one comes from
  • A decision table: what to do when \(a\) depends on \(t\), \(v\) or \(s\)
  • Choosing the limits of integration
  • Reading and drawing motion graphs

A particle moving along a straight line needs only one number to say where it is: its position \(s\), measured from a fixed origin, with one direction chosen as positive. Every idea in the rest of the course is a dressed-up version of this chapter, so it pays to get it rock solid.

Three definitions

\[ v = \frac{ds}{dt} \qquad\qquad a = \frac{dv}{dt} \qquad\qquad a\,ds = v\,dv \]

The first two are definitions: velocity is how fast position changes, and acceleration is how fast velocity changes. The third is not a new law. It is the second one rewritten with the chain rule:

\[ a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{ds}\cdot\frac{ds}{dt} = \frac{dv}{ds}\,v \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a\,ds = v\,dv \]
Why we need the third one

Sometimes the acceleration is given as a function of position, as with a spring, which pushes harder the further you stretch it. Then \(a = dv/dt\) is useless, because you cannot integrate a function of \(s\) with respect to \(t\). The chain-rule form swaps time out for position, so you can separate the variables and integrate.

Which equation? Look at what \(a\) depends on

The single most useful question in L02–L03 is “what is the acceleration a function of?” The answer tells you which equation to separate.

GivenUseSeparate asYou get
\(a\) constantthe constant-\(a\) equations(already integrated)\(v=v_0+at,\ s=s_0+v_0t+\tfrac12at^2,\ v^2=v_0^2+2a(s-s_0)\)
\(a(t)\)\(a = dv/dt\)\(\int dv = \int a(t)\,dt\)\(v(t)\), then \(s(t)\) from \(v=ds/dt\)
\(a(v)\)\(a=dv/dt\) or \(a\,ds=v\,dv\)\(\int \frac{dv}{a(v)}=\int dt\) or \(\int\frac{v\,dv}{a(v)} = \int ds\)time or distance, whichever is asked
\(a(s)\)\(a\,ds = v\,dv\)\(\int a(s)\,ds = \int v\,dv\)\(v(s)\)
Common slip

The constant-acceleration equations are only allowed when \(a\) really is constant. L03’s key outputs say it plainly: acceleration does not have to be constant. If \(a\) contains \(t\), \(v\) or \(s\), you must integrate.

Choosing limits of integration

Each integral has limits on both sides, and the limits on the two sides must describe the same two moments. The lower limits are the starting state, and the upper limits are the state you want.

\[ \int_{v_0}^{v} dv = \int_{0}^{t} a\,dt \qquad\text{reads as}\qquad \text{“from when the speed was } v_0 \text{ at } t=0, \text{ to when it is } v \text{ at time } t\text{”} \]

If you know the end state (say the particle stops, so \(v = 0\)), put that number in as the upper limit directly.

Worked example 2.1: acceleration that depends on time

Final exam 2019, Q1 (Review lecture 2)

A particle is fired into a long test chamber at \(v_0 = 27\) m/s when \(t = 0\). Its acceleration is \(a = -6t\) m/s². Ignoring gravity, how far does it travel before it stops?

  1. \(a\) depends on \(t\), so start from \(a = dv/dt\) and separate:
    \[ \int_{27}^{v} dv = \int_0^t -6t\,dt \;\Rightarrow\; v = 27 - 3t^2 \]
    Time is the variable we know \(a\) in terms of, so time has to be the variable we integrate over.
  2. Find when it stops: \(0 = 27 - 3t^2 \Rightarrow t = 3\) s.“Stops” is a velocity condition, so use the velocity equation to turn it into a time.
  3. Integrate again for position:
    \[ \int_0^x ds = \int_0^3 (27 - 3t^2)\,dt = \big[27t - t^3\big]_0^3 = 81 - 27 \]
    \(v = ds/dt\), and \(v\) is now a known function of time.

x = 54.0 m

Check: the velocity never changes sign before \(t = 3\) s, so distance travelled equals displacement.

Worked example 2.2: acceleration that depends on velocity (drag)

Same idea as Tut01 Q3–Q4

A boat cuts its engine at 20 m/s. Water drag gives \(a = -0.05\,v^2\) m/s². How far does it coast, and how long does it take, to slow to 10 m/s?

  1. Distance: the question links speed to distance, so use \(a\,ds = v\,dv\):
    \[ \int_0^s ds = \int_{20}^{10}\frac{v\,dv}{-0.05v^2} = -20\big[\ln v\big]_{20}^{10} = 20\ln 2 \]
    \(a\) is a function of \(v\). The \(v\,dv\) form gives distance directly, without going through time.
  2. Time: use \(a = dv/dt\):
    \[ \int_0^t dt = \int_{20}^{10}\frac{dv}{-0.05v^2} = 20\Big[\frac1v\Big]_{20}^{10} = 20(0.1 - 0.05) \]
    Same \(a(v)\), but now time is wanted, so put \(dt\) on the other side.

s = 13.9 m, t = 1.00 s

Worked example 2.3: constant acceleration

L02 homework, M&K 2/14

A ball is thrown straight up at 30 m/s from the edge of a 60 m cliff. Find the height \(h\) it rises above the edge, and the time to reach the bottom of the cliff.

  1. Take up as positive, so \(a = -9.81\) m/s², which is constant.Gravity is the only acceleration, and near the Earth it does not change. That is the one situation where the constant-\(a\) equations are legal.
  2. At the top, \(v = 0\): \(0 = 30^2 - 2(9.81)h \Rightarrow h = 45.9\) m.We know speeds and want a distance, so use the equation without \(t\) in it.
  3. The bottom is at \(s = -60\) m: \(-60 = 30t - 4.905t^2\). Solve the quadratic and keep the positive root: \(t = 7.70\) s.Measuring \(s\) from the cliff edge means the bottom is negative. Signs carry the direction, so there is no need to split the trip into up and down legs.

h = 45.9 m (matches the homework answer), t = 7.70 s

Motion graphs

L03 treats graphs as calculus you can see. Two facts do all the work: the slope of a graph is the next quantity down the chain, and the area under a graph is the change in the quantity above it.

From this graphSlope givesArea gives
\(s\)–\(t\)\(v\)
\(v\)–\(t\)\(a\)\(\Delta s\)
\(a\)–\(t\)\(\Delta v\)
\(v\)–\(s\)\(a = v\,\frac{dv}{ds}\) (slope times height)
\(a\)–\(s\)\(\tfrac12(v^2 - v_0^2)\)
Why the a–s area gives ½v²

Integrate \(a\,ds = v\,dv\) on both sides: \(\int a\,ds = \tfrac12 v^2 - \tfrac12 v_0^2\). So the area under an \(a\)–\(s\) graph is not a velocity. It is the change in \(\tfrac12v^2\). That is exactly how you build the \(v\)–\(s\) graph in Tut01 Q2: add up the area as you go, then take a square root.

Drawing a graph from the one above it: a checklist

  1. Split the time axis wherever the given graph changes formula.
  2. Integrating raises the power by one. A constant becomes a sloped line, and a sloped line becomes a parabola.
  3. Carry the end value of each piece into the start of the next. The curve never jumps (unless there is an impact).
  4. Label the key values at every break point, and mark maxima. Where \(v=0\), the \(s\)–\(t\) curve is flat.
In one breath
  • \(v=ds/dt\), \(a=dv/dt\), \(a\,ds=v\,dv\). The third is the chain rule.
  • Ask what \(a\) depends on, then separate the matching equation.
  • Limits on both sides describe the same two moments.
  • Slope goes down the chain, area goes back up it.
Chapter 3 · Lectures L04–L08

Curved paths: three ways to look at the same motion

In this chapter
  • Rectangular (x–y) components and projectiles
  • Normal–tangential (n–t) components: the key to everything that turns
  • Polar (r–θ) components and the strange-looking Coriolis term
  • Cylindrical and spherical coordinates for 3D
The big idea

The motion is the same whichever coordinates you use. You only choose the coordinate system that makes your problem easy. Use x–y when the forces line up with fixed directions (gravity). Use n–t when you know the path and the speed along it. Use r–θ when something is measured from a fixed point, such as a rotating arm, a radar, or a slot.

One fact holds in every system: velocity is always tangent to the path. Acceleration usually is not, and the three systems are just three ways of splitting it into pieces.

Rectangular components (L04)

\[ \vec r = x\hat i + y\hat j \qquad \vec v = \dot x\,\hat i + \dot y\,\hat j \qquad \vec a = \ddot x\,\hat i + \ddot y\,\hat j \]

Because \(\hat i\) and \(\hat j\) never change direction, you differentiate each component on its own. A curved motion splits into two straight-line motions, each of which is a Chapter 2 problem.

Projectiles are the classic case. With no air resistance, \(a_x = 0\) and \(a_y = -g\).

\[ x = x_0 + v_{0x}t \qquad v_y = v_{0y} - gt \qquad y = y_0 + v_{0y}t - \tfrac12 g t^2 \qquad v_y^2 = v_{0y}^2 - 2g(y-y_0) \]
Why the horizontal speed never changes

Gravity pulls straight down. Nothing pushes sideways, so nothing changes the sideways velocity. The only thing the horizontal and vertical motions share is the clock. Time is the link you solve for, usually from the vertical equation, and then use in the horizontal one.

Worked example 3.1: a simple projectile

Tut02 Q1 uses the same method

A ball is kicked from level ground at 20 m/s, 35° above horizontal. Find its range and maximum height.

  1. Split the launch velocity: \(v_{0x} = 20\cos35^\circ = 16.38\) m/s and \(v_{0y} = 20\sin35^\circ = 11.47\) m/s.
  2. Time of flight: it lands when \(y = 0\) again, so \(0 = 11.47t - 4.905t^2 \Rightarrow t = 2.339\) s.The vertical motion decides when it lands. The horizontal motion only tells you where.
  3. Range: \(x = 16.38 \times 2.339 = 38.3\) m. Maximum height (where \(v_y = 0\)): \(H = 11.47^2/(2\times 9.81) = 6.71\) m.

Range 38.3 m, maximum height 6.71 m

Normal and tangential components (L05)

Ride along with the particle. One unit vector \(\hat e_t\) points forward along the path, and the other, \(\hat e_n\), points sideways towards the centre of curvature (the inside of the bend).

\[ \vec v = v\,\hat e_t \qquad\qquad \vec a = \underbrace{\dot v\,\hat e_t}_{a_t} + \underbrace{\frac{v^2}{\rho}\,\hat e_n}_{a_n} \]
Why two pieces, and why v²/ρ

Velocity can change in two ways: it can get longer or shorter (speed changes), or it can turn (direction changes). Each kind of change needs its own acceleration.

  • \(a_t = \dot v = dv/dt\) changes the speed. It is zero when you drive round a bend at a constant speed.
  • \(a_n = v^2/\rho\) changes the direction. It always points into the bend. Going twice as fast round the same bend turns the velocity twice as quickly and the velocity is twice as big, so \(a_n\) goes up four times. That is why \(v\) appears squared. A tighter bend (smaller \(\rho\)) turns you faster, so \(\rho\) is on the bottom.

Unless the speed is changing, \(a_n\) is the only acceleration, which is why you feel pushed outwards in a turning car.

For a path given as \(y(x)\), the radius of curvature is \(\rho = \frac{\left[1+(dy/dx)^2\right]^{3/2}}{|d^2y/dx^2|}\) (the hint in Tut02 Q2). On a circle, \(\rho\) is just the radius, and that special case drives all of rigid-body rotation (Chapter 6).

Worked example 3.2: a car on a bend

Like L05 Example 1

A car rounds a bend of radius 50 m at 20 m/s and is speeding up at 3 m/s². Find the size of its acceleration.

  1. \(a_t = \dot v = 3\) m/s² (given directly as the rate of change of speed).
  2. \(a_n = v^2/\rho = 20^2/50 = 8\) m/s², pointing to the centre of the bend.
  3. The two are perpendicular, so \(a = \sqrt{3^2 + 8^2}\).\(\hat e_t\) and \(\hat e_n\) are at right angles, so Pythagoras applies.

a = 8.54 m/s²

Polar coordinates (L06–L07)

Now describe the particle by its distance \(r\) from a fixed point O and the angle \(\theta\) of the line OP. The unit vectors are \(\hat e_r\) (straight out along OP) and \(\hat e_\theta\) (a quarter-turn anticlockwise from it).

\[ \vec v = \dot r\,\hat e_r + r\dot\theta\,\hat e_\theta \qquad\qquad \vec a = \big(\ddot r - r\dot\theta^2\big)\hat e_r + \big(r\ddot\theta + 2\dot r\dot\theta\big)\hat e_\theta \]
What each term means
  • \(\dot r\): sliding outwards along the arm. \(r\dot\theta\): being carried round by the arm, like a point at radius \(r\) on a wheel spinning at \(\dot\theta\).
  • \(\ddot r\): the outward slide speeding up.
  • \(-r\dot\theta^2\): the centripetal term (the \(v^2/\rho\) of a circle). It is negative because it points inwards, towards O.
  • \(r\ddot\theta\): the arm spinning faster.
  • \(2\dot r\dot\theta\): the Coriolis term. Two things happen when you slide outward on a spinning arm. You move to a bigger radius, where the same \(\dot\theta\) means a faster sideways speed. And your outward velocity is itself being swung round. Each effect contributes one \(\dot r\dot\theta\), so the term is \(2\dot r\dot\theta\).

Worked example 3.3: a collar on a rotating rod

Same set-up as Tut02 Q3–Q4

A rod spins at a constant \(\dot\theta = 2\) rad/s. A collar on it is at \(r = 0.5\) m and sliding outward at a steady \(\dot r = 0.3\) m/s. Find the collar’s velocity and acceleration.

  1. List the five numbers you need: \(r = 0.5\), \(\dot r = 0.3\), \(\ddot r = 0\), \(\dot\theta = 2\), \(\ddot\theta = 0\).Every polar question comes down to finding these five numbers. The formulas do the rest.
  2. \(v_r = 0.3\) m/s and \(v_\theta = 0.5\times2 = 1.0\) m/s, so \(v = \sqrt{0.3^2+1.0^2} = 1.04\) m/s.
  3. \(a_r = 0 - 0.5(2)^2 = -2.0\) m/s² (inwards) and \(a_\theta = 0 + 2(0.3)(2) = 1.2\) m/s², so \(a = 2.33\) m/s².Even with nothing speeding up, there are two accelerations: the inward centripetal one, and the Coriolis one from sliding outward on a spinning rod.

v = 1.04 m/s, a = 2.33 m/s²

3D: cylindrical and spherical (L08)

Cylindrical coordinates are polar coordinates with a height \(z\) added. Use them for helices (the roller coaster in L04) and anything turning around a vertical axis while rising.

\[ \vec v = \dot r\,\hat e_r + r\dot\theta\,\hat e_\theta + \dot z\,\hat k \qquad \vec a = (\ddot r - r\dot\theta^2)\hat e_r + (r\ddot\theta + 2\dot r\dot\theta)\hat e_\theta + \ddot z\,\hat k \]

Spherical coordinates \((R, \theta, \phi)\) suit radar antennas and anything pointing into the sky, like latitude (\(\phi\), measured up from the horizontal plane) and longitude (\(\theta\)). The velocity, as in L08, is

\[ \vec v = \dot R\,\hat e_R + R\dot\theta\cos\phi\,\hat e_\theta + R\dot\phi\,\hat e_\phi \]

and the acceleration components are

\[ a_R = \ddot R - R\dot\phi^2 - R\dot\theta^2\cos^2\phi \qquad a_\theta = \frac{\cos\phi}{R}\frac{d}{dt}\!\left(R^2\dot\theta\right) - 2R\dot\theta\dot\phi\sin\phi \qquad a_\phi = \frac1R\frac{d}{dt}\!\left(R^2\dot\phi\right) + R\dot\theta^2\sin\phi\cos\phi \]

You are not expected to derive these. Learn to list \(R, \dot R, \ddot R, \theta, \dot\theta, \ddot\theta, \phi, \dot\phi, \ddot\phi\) carefully, just as for polar coordinates, and then substitute.

In one breath
  • Velocity is always tangent to the path. Choose coordinates to suit the problem.
  • x–y: components are independent, and time links them.
  • n–t: \(a_t = \dot v\) changes the speed and \(a_n = v^2/\rho\) turns the velocity into the bend.
  • r–θ: list the five numbers, then use \((\ddot r - r\dot\theta^2)\) and \((r\ddot\theta + 2\dot r\dot\theta)\).
Chapter 4 · Lecture L09

Relative motion: what one moving observer sees

In this chapter
  • The relative-motion equation and how to read the subscripts
  • Your first vector triangle, drawn step by step
  • Relative acceleration with n–t components
The big idea

Picture yourself in car A, watching car B. What you see (B relative to A) is B’s real motion with your own motion taken away. Written the other way round, B’s real motion is your motion plus what you see. That one sentence is the equation for the whole chapter, and for Chapters 9 and 10 as well.

\[ \vec r_B = \vec r_A + \vec r_{B/A} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \vec v_B = \vec v_A + \vec v_{B/A} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \vec a_B = \vec a_A + \vec a_{B/A} \]

Read \(\vec v_{B/A}\) as “the velocity of B as seen from A”. The second and third equations are just the first one differentiated, once and twice. In L09 the observer’s axes translate but do not rotate. The observer slides along with A but keeps facing north.

Why it is just addition

Positions add like steps on a map: getting from O to B is the same as getting from O to A and then from A to B. Differentiating a sum gives the sum of the derivatives, so velocities and accelerations add the same way. Nothing more is going on.

Two habits that prevent most mistakes:

  • \(\vec v_{A/B} = -\vec v_{B/A}\). Swapping the letters flips the arrow and keeps the size.
  • The equation is one vector equation, so it is worth two scalar equations (\(x\) and \(y\)). At most two things can be unknown.

Drawing the vector triangle

The equation \(\vec v_B = \vec v_A + \vec v_{B/A}\) is a triangle. Draw \(\vec v_A\) first. Put the tail of \(\vec v_{B/A}\) at the tip of \(\vec v_A\). The line from the start to the final tip is \(\vec v_B\). Read it like a journey: go along \(\vec v_A\), then along \(\vec v_{B/A}\), and you arrive where \(\vec v_B\) takes you directly.

Worked example 4.1: two cars at a crossing

Same method as L09 Examples 1 and 3, Tut03 Q2

Car A drives east at 20 m/s. Car B drives north at 15 m/s on the crossing road. What velocity does B appear to have to the driver of A?

  1. Size, from the right angle at o: \(v_{B/A} = \sqrt{20^2 + 15^2} = 25.0\) m/s.With no right angle, you would use the cosine rule (Chapter 1).
  2. Direction: \(\tan^{-1}(15/20) = 36.9^\circ\) north of west. In the course’s angle notation that is \(\measuredangle\,143.1^\circ\).
  3. Check with components, which matches:
    \[ \vec v_{B/A} = \vec v_B - \vec v_A = (0, 15) - (20, 0) = (-20, 15)\ \text{m/s} \]

vB/A = 25.0 m/s at 36.9° north of west

It makes sense physically: to the driver of A, the whole world drifts west at 20 m/s, so B appears to move north and west.

Relative acceleration

The same triangle works for accelerations. The extra step is that a particle on a curved path has two acceleration components (Chapter 3), and you must include both.

\[ (\vec a_B)_n + (\vec a_B)_t = \vec a_A + \vec a_{B/A} \]

Worked example 4.2: the cars again, with B on a bend

Like L09 Example 3

At the same instant, A is speeding up at 2 m/s². B is on a bend of radius 100 m curving towards the west and is slowing down at 1 m/s². Find \(\vec a_{B/A}\).

  1. \(\vec a_A = 2\) m/s² east, along its straight path.
  2. \((a_B)_n = v_B^2/\rho = 15^2/100 = 2.25\) m/s², pointing into the bend (west).B is turning, so part of its acceleration must point towards the centre of the bend.
  3. \((a_B)_t = 1\) m/s² pointing south, opposite to its motion, because B is slowing down.
  4. Subtract:
    \[ \vec a_{B/A} = \vec a_B - \vec a_A = (-2.25, -1) - (2, 0) = (-4.25, -1)\ \text{m/s}^2 \]

aB/A = 4.37 m/s² at ∡ −166.8° (13.2° south of west)

In one breath
  • \(\vec v_B = \vec v_A + \vec v_{B/A}\): B’s real motion is A’s motion plus what A sees.
  • Draw the absolute vectors from one point o. The relative vector joins their tips.
  • For a curved path, split acceleration into \(n\) (\(v^2/\rho\), into the bend) and \(t\).
  • A 2D vector equation can solve for at most two unknowns.
Chapter 5 · Lecture L10

Pulleys: motion tied together by a rope

In this chapter
  • The rope-length method (position coordinates)
  • The quick “velocity line” method for pulleys
  • Why a pulley is secretly a rolling wheel
The big idea

A rope does not stretch. Its total length is a constant, so if you write that length in terms of the positions of the blocks and differentiate, the constant disappears. What remains links the velocities, and differentiating again links the accelerations.

Method 1: the rope-length equation

  1. Datums. Measure each moving thing’s position (\(s_A\), \(s_B\), …) from a fixed line, usually through the centre of a fixed pulley. Choose positive in the direction each thing moves (often “down”).
  2. Length. Add up the rope segments that change length. Leave out bits that never change, such as the arcs wrapped round pulleys. A pulley hanging in a loop of rope contributes its coordinate twice, once for each side of the loop.
  3. More than one rope? Write one length equation per rope, then eliminate the shared coordinate.
  4. Differentiate. Constants vanish. Watch the signs: a negative answer means opposite to your positive direction.
Why a pulley’s coordinate counts twice

If a moving pulley hangs in a loop of rope and drops by 1 cm, both rope segments beside it get 1 cm longer. That 2 cm has to come from somewhere else in the rope. This is where every factor of 2 in pulley problems comes from: the block on a moving pulley moves at half the speed of the free end.

Worked example 5.1: two ropes

L10 Example 2: keep the slide’s figure open

The rope at A is pulled down at 2 m/s. Find the speed of block B.

  1. Datum through the fixed top pulley, with all coordinates positive downwards. There are three moving things: the end A, pulley C and block B.
  2. Rope 1 (A round to C): \(s_A + 2s_C = l_1\).Pulley C hangs in a loop of rope 1, so \(s_C\) appears twice.
  3. Rope 2 (C round B): \(s_B + (s_B - s_C) = l_2\).One segment runs from the datum to B. The other runs from C down to B, and its length is the gap \(s_B - s_C\).
  4. Eliminate \(s_C\): doubling rope 2 gives \(4s_B - 2s_C = 2l_2\), and adding rope 1 gives \(s_A + 4s_B = l_1 + 2l_2\).
  5. Differentiate: \(v_A + 4v_B = 0 \Rightarrow v_B = -\tfrac14 (2) = -0.5\) m/s.

vB = 0.5 m/s upwards

The minus sign says B moves against the “positive down” direction, so it rises.

Method 2: the velocity line (velocity analysis)

L10 shows a much faster method that uses one fact: across a pulley, velocity changes in a straight line. Draw the pulley with a horizontal diameter, put the rope speeds as arrows at the two edges, and join their tips with a straight line. The height of that line at the centre is the speed of the pulley’s axle.

\[ v_{\text{centre}} = \frac{v_{\text{left}} + v_{\text{right}}}{2} \qquad \text{(with signs: up positive)} \]
Why the line is straight

The rope grips the pulley, so the pulley’s rim moves with the rope wherever they touch. A pulley is a rigid disc, so its velocities vary linearly across it, just like a wheel rolling along the rope. If one side of the rope is fixed, that side of the pulley is momentarily still. It is the pulley’s instantaneous centre (Chapter 8), and the speed grows in proportion to the distance from it.

  • Fixed pulley (axle fixed): the line passes through the centre, so the two rope sides move at equal speeds in opposite directions.
  • Movable pulley, one side tied: the centre moves at half the speed of the free side.
  • Both sides moving: the centre moves at the average. In L10 Example 4, A moves down at 4 m/s and C moves up at 2 m/s, so B moves at \((4-2)/2 = 1\) m/s.

Work from the pulley you know most about towards the one you want, carrying each answer across shared ropes.

In one breath
  • Rope length is constant, so differentiate the length equation.
  • A pulley in a loop of rope counts twice, which gives the factors of 2.
  • Velocity line: rope speeds at the edges, a straight line between the tips, read off the centre.
  • Practice: L10 Examples 3–5 and Tut03 Q1.
Chapter 6 · Lecture L11

Rigid bodies: spinning about a fixed axis

In this chapter
  • The three kinds of planar motion
  • Angular position, velocity and acceleration
  • The three formulas for any point on a spinning body: \(v=\omega r\), \(a_n=\omega^2 r\), \(a_t=\alpha r\)
  • Gears and belts

From here on, objects have size. A rigid body never changes shape: the distance between any two of its points stays the same. That one property is what makes everything in Chapters 6 to 10 work.

Three kinds of planar motion

  • Translation: every line on the body stays parallel to itself. It can be rectilinear (straight paths) or curvilinear (curved paths). Either way, every point has the same velocity and acceleration, so the body behaves like one particle.
  • Rotation about a fixed axis: every point moves on a circle round the axis (a crank, a gear, a door).
  • General plane motion: translation and rotation at once (a connecting rod, a rolling wheel, a sliding ladder, a thrown Frisbee). This is where Chapters 7 to 10 live.

Angular motion is Chapter 2 again

Replace \(s, v, a\) by \(\theta, \omega, \alpha\) and every rectilinear result carries straight over:

\[ \omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt} \qquad \alpha = \frac{d\omega}{dt} \qquad \omega\,d\omega = \alpha\,d\theta \]
\[ \text{constant }\alpha:\quad \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t \qquad \Delta\theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac12\alpha t^2 \qquad \omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\,\Delta\theta \]

Anticlockwise is positive. Use the same decision table as in Chapter 2: ask whether \(\alpha\) is given as a function of \(t\), \(\omega\) or \(\theta\). (The 2019 exam pulley question gives \(\alpha = 0.8\theta\), so it needs \(\omega\,d\omega = \alpha\,d\theta\).)

A point on a spinning body

\[ v = \omega r \quad(\perp OP) \qquad\qquad a_n = \omega^2 r \quad(\text{towards }O) \qquad\qquad a_t = \alpha r \quad(\perp OP) \]
Why these three

P moves on a circle of radius \(r\), so this is just n–t motion (Chapter 3) with \(\rho = r\).

  • In one radian of turn, P travels a distance \(r\). Turning at \(\omega\) rad/s, it travels \(\omega r\) metres per second.
  • \(a_n = v^2/\rho = (\omega r)^2/r = \omega^2 r\). It always points to the centre, because the velocity is being turned towards it.
  • \(a_t = \dot v = \frac{d}{dt}(\omega r) = \alpha r\), because \(r\) is fixed.

In vector form these are \(\vec v = \vec\omega\times\vec r\), \(\vec a_n = \vec\omega\times(\vec\omega\times\vec r) = -\omega^2\vec r\) and \(\vec a_t = \vec\alpha\times\vec r\). These are the Chapter 1 cross product turning \(\vec r\) a quarter-turn.

Common slip

If a crank turns at constant \(\omega\), then \(\alpha = 0\) and \(a_t = 0\), but \(a_n = \omega^2 r\) is not zero. A point moving at steady speed round a circle is still accelerating, towards the centre. Forgetting this costs marks in every relative acceleration question.

Gears and belts

Where two wheels touch without slipping, or are joined by a belt, the touching points share the same speed and the same tangential acceleration:

\[ \omega_A r_A = \omega_B r_B \qquad\qquad \alpha_A r_A = \alpha_B r_B \]

Their normal accelerations differ, because \(\omega^2 r\) depends on each wheel’s own \(\omega\) and \(r\) (L17, “bodies in contact”).

Worked example 6.1: belt drive starting from rest

Like L11 Example 1 and Tut03 Q4

Pulley A (radius 50 mm) starts from rest with \(\alpha_A = 6t\) rad/s². A belt drives pulley B (radius 150 mm). At \(t = 2\) s, find \(\omega_B\), the angle B has turned, and the acceleration of a point on B’s rim.

  1. \(\alpha\) depends on \(t\), so integrate: \(\omega_A = \int_0^t 6t\,dt = 3t^2 = 12\) rad/s at \(t=2\), and \(\theta_A = \int_0^t 3t^2\,dt = t^3 = 8\) rad.
  2. The belt links the rims: \(\omega_B = \omega_A r_A/r_B = 12\times50/150 = 4.00\) rad/s, and in the same ratio \(\theta_B = 8/3 = 2.67\) rad and \(\alpha_B = 12/3 = 4\) rad/s².The belt does not stretch or slip, so both rims move the same distance, at the same speed, with the same tangential acceleration.
  3. Rim of B: \(a_t = \alpha_B r_B = 4(0.15) = 0.60\) m/s² and \(a_n = \omega_B^2 r_B = 16(0.15) = 2.40\) m/s², so \(a = \sqrt{0.6^2 + 2.4^2}\).

ωB = 4.00 rad/s, θB = 2.67 rad, a = 2.47 m/s²

In one breath
  • Rigid means fixed distances between points.
  • \(\theta, \omega, \alpha\) follow exactly the same rules as \(s, v, a\).
  • A point on a spinning body: \(v=\omega r\) and \(a_t=\alpha r\), both ⟂ to the radius, plus \(a_n=\omega^2r\) towards the axis.
  • Gears and belts share \(v\) and \(a_t\) at the contact, not \(a_n\).
Chapter 7 · Lecture L12

Absolute motion: write the geometry, then differentiate

In this chapter
  • The four-step tactic from L12
  • The sliding ladder and the slider-crank done by calculus
  • Rolling without slipping: \(s = r\theta\)
The big idea

If you can write where a point is as a formula in an angle, you can find how fast it moves by differentiating. The chain rule does the work: every time you differentiate a \(\theta\), a \(\dot\theta = \omega\) appears.

The tactic (from L12)

  1. Locate the point with a coordinate \(s\) measured from a fixed origin.
  2. Measure the angle \(\theta\) of a line in the body from a fixed reference line, and use the body’s dimensions to write \(s = f(\theta)\).
  3. Differentiate once to get \(v\) in terms of \(\omega = \dot\theta\).
  4. Differentiate again to get \(a\) in terms of \(\omega\) and \(\alpha = \ddot\theta\). Use the product rule, because \(\dot\theta\) can itself change.

Worked example 7.1: the sliding ladder

The same bar as L14 Example 1, solved by calculus

A 1.5 m bar has end A on the floor and end B on a wall. A slides away from the wall at 3 m/s. When the bar makes 30° with the floor, find \(\omega\) and the velocity of B.

  1. Geometry, with \(\theta\) the angle at A between the floor and the bar: \(x_A = 1.5\cos\theta\) (from the wall) and \(y_B = 1.5\sin\theta\) (up the wall).Both ends are tied to one angle by the fixed length of the bar.
  2. Differentiate \(x_A\): \(\dot x_A = -1.5\sin\theta\,\dot\theta\). Put in \(\dot x_A = 3\): \(3 = -1.5(0.5)\dot\theta \Rightarrow \dot\theta = -4\) rad/s.The minus sign means \(\theta\) is getting smaller, so the bar is falling flatter, which makes sense as A slides out.
  3. Differentiate \(y_B\): \(\dot y_B = 1.5\cos\theta\,\dot\theta = 1.5(0.866)(-4) = -5.20\) m/s.

|ω| = 4.00 rad/s, vB = 5.20 m/s down the wall

Keep these numbers in mind. Chapter 8 gets them from a single point, and Chapter 9 from a triangle.

Worked example 7.2: slider-crank

L12 Example 3

Crank AB (0.2 m) turns at a constant 150 rad/s. Connecting rod BP is 0.75 m, and P slides along the horizontal line through A. Find the velocity of P when \(\theta = 30^\circ\).

  1. Geometry: \(x_P = \underbrace{0.2\cos\theta}_{\text{crank}} + \underbrace{\sqrt{0.75^2 - (0.2\sin\theta)^2}}_{\text{rod, by Pythagoras}}\).The rod’s horizontal reach comes from its length and the height of B above the slider line.
  2. Differentiate with the chain rule:
    \[ v_P = -0.2\omega\sin\theta - \frac{0.2^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\omega}{\sqrt{0.75^2 - (0.2\sin\theta)^2}} \]
  3. Substitute: \(v_P = -15.0 - \frac{2.598}{0.7433} = -15.0 - 3.50\).

vP = 18.5 m/s towards A

Rolling without slipping

A wheel that rolls without slipping lays its rim down on the ground like tape off a roll. After turning through \(\theta\), the centre has moved exactly the length of rim that touched the ground:

\[ s_O = r\theta \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v_O = r\omega \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad a_O = r\alpha \]

L12 Example 4 follows a point on the rim and finds that, at the moment it touches the ground, its velocity is zero but its acceleration is \(r\omega^2\) upwards. Remember this: it comes back in Chapters 8 and 10.

When to choose this method

Absolute motion is ideal when the geometry is simple and you want a formula valid at every angle (for example a cam follower, L12 Example 2). It becomes painful when the expression is messy, and differentiating it twice for acceleration is where mistakes creep in. For linkages at one instant, the relative velocity diagram (Chapter 9) is usually faster, and it is what the exams ask for.

In one breath
  • Write position as a function of the angle, using fixed origins.
  • Differentiate with the chain rule; every \(d\theta/dt\) is \(\omega\).
  • Rolling without slip: \(s=r\theta\), \(v=r\omega\), \(a=r\alpha\).
  • Practice: L12 Questions 1–2 and Tut03 Q3.
Chapter 8 · Lecture L13

The instantaneous centre: pretend it is just spinning

In this chapter
  • What the instantaneous centre (IC) is, and why it always exists
  • Three ways to find it
  • Fast velocity answers from one distance
  • The trap: the IC is not a point of zero acceleration
The big idea

At any single instant, a body in plane motion moves as if it were spinning about one point. That point has zero velocity at that instant, and it is called the instantaneous centre of zero velocity (IC). Find it, and every velocity on the body is just \(v = \omega \times (\text{distance to the IC})\), perpendicular to the line to the IC. This is the Chapter 6 formula, borrowed for one moment.

Finding the IC

Every velocity on the body is perpendicular to the line joining that point to the IC. Turned around, the IC must lie on the perpendicular to each velocity. That gives three cases:

  1. You know \(\vec v_A\) and \(\omega\): the IC is on the perpendicular to \(\vec v_A\) through A, at distance \(v_A/\omega\).
  2. You know the directions of two velocities (the usual case: a slider, or a pin on a crank): draw the perpendicular to each through its point. The IC is where they cross.
  3. Two parallel velocities, perpendicular to the line joining their points: use similar triangles. The IC is where the line through the arrow tips meets the line through the points. If the two velocities are equal, the lines never meet: the body is translating, the IC is “at infinity”, and \(\omega = 0\).

Worked example 8.1: the sliding ladder in one line

Same bar as Chapters 7 and 9
  1. Distances from the IC: \(r_{A/IC} = 1.5\sin30^\circ = 0.75\) m and \(r_{B/IC} = 1.5\cos30^\circ = 1.30\) m.
  2. \(\omega = v_A / r_{A/IC} = 3/0.75 = 4.00\) rad/s. A moves right while sitting below the IC, so the bar turns anticlockwise about it.Imagine the bar pinned at the IC. For the point below the pin to move right, the bar must turn anticlockwise.
  3. \(v_B = \omega\, r_{B/IC} = 4(1.30) = 5.20\) m/s. B is to the left of the IC, so with anticlockwise rotation it moves down.

ω = 4.00 rad/s CCW, vB = 5.20 m/s ↓ (the same as Chapter 7)

L13 Example 1 does the slider-crank from Chapter 7 the same way and gets \(v_P = 18.5\) m/s again. You now have three methods that give one answer, which is a good sign the physics is consistent.

Rolling wheels

A wheel rolling without slip has its IC at the contact point C, because that point is momentarily stuck to the ground. So the centre moves at \(\omega r\), and the top of the wheel moves at \(\omega(2r) = 2v_O\). The top of a bicycle tyre really does move at twice the bike’s speed.

The trap

The IC has zero velocity, not zero acceleration. A moment later, a different point is the IC. The contact point of a rolling wheel accelerates at \(\omega^2 r\) straight up, towards the centre (L12 Example 4, L17). So never take moments of acceleration about the IC and never use \(a = \alpha \times (\text{distance to IC})\). For accelerations, use the relative acceleration diagram (Chapter 10).

Why an IC always exists

Chapter 9 shows that any point’s velocity is a reference point’s velocity plus \(\omega\times\) the relative position. Whenever \(\omega\neq 0\), you can always find one position where the spin part exactly cancels the reference velocity. That position is the IC. When \(\omega = 0\) there is nothing to cancel with, so there is no IC (it is at infinity) and the body translates.

In one breath
  • The IC is the point momentarily at rest. Every velocity is \(\omega\times\) the distance to it, perpendicular to the line to it.
  • Find it where the perpendiculars to two known velocity directions cross.
  • Parallel equal velocities put the IC at infinity, so \(\omega = 0\).
  • Never use the IC for accelerations.
  • Practice: L13 Examples 2–4 and Tut03 Q5.
Chapter 9 · Lectures L14–L15 · the heart of the book, part 1

Relative velocity: drawing the velocity diagram

In this chapter
  • The one equation, and why the relative velocity is always perpendicular to the bar
  • The known/unknown audit that tells you a diagram will close
  • A ten-step recipe for drawing the diagram, with the reason for each step
  • How to tell clockwise from anticlockwise straight from your diagram
  • Four worked examples, three of them past exam questions

The one equation

Take any two points A and B on the same rigid body. Chapter 4 already says \(\vec v_B = \vec v_A + \vec v_{B/A}\). What is new is that, on a rigid body, we know a great deal about \(\vec v_{B/A}\) before we start:

\[ \vec v_B = \vec v_A + \vec v_{B/A} \qquad\text{where}\qquad \vec v_{B/A} = \vec\omega\times\vec r_{B/A},\quad v_{B/A} = \omega\,r_{AB},\quad \vec v_{B/A}\perp AB \]
Why the relative velocity is perpendicular to the bar

Sit at A, move with it, but do not turn. B is always exactly \(r_{AB}\) away from you, because the body is rigid. A point that stays a fixed distance from you can only move around you on a circle. A velocity on a circle is tangent to it, so \(\vec v_{B/A}\) is perpendicular to AB. Its size is \(\omega r_{AB}\), because that is how fast a point on a circle of radius \(r_{AB}\) moves when the radius turns at \(\omega\) (Chapter 6).

So the general plane motion of any rigid body is a translation (everything moving with A) plus a rotation about A (L14, “interpretation of relative velocity”).

This is why the relative velocity diagram works so well. One of the three vectors always has a known direction (perpendicular to the bar) without any calculation. That direction is the green dashed line in every diagram below.

Choose points you know something about

The equation is only useful if A and B are points whose motion you already partly know. In practice these are almost always pins and sliders:

Type of pointDirection of its velocitySize
Pin on a crank that turns about a fixed pivot⟂ to the crank\(\omega_{\text{crank}}\,r\) if \(\omega\) is given, otherwise unknown
Slider (piston, collar, block) in a straight guideAlong the guideUsually unknown
Contact point of a wheel rolling without slipZero, so it makes a great reference point
Centre of a rolling wheelParallel to the surface\(\omega r\)
Pin joining two barsOne velocity, shared by both bars. This is how you carry an answer from one bar to the next.

The audit: will the diagram close?

Every vector has two pieces of information, a size and a direction. A 2D vector equation gives two scalar equations, so at most two pieces can be unknown. Before drawing anything, fill in a small table. Exam memos award ticks for exactly this table, written next to the equation.

TermSizeDirection
\(\vec v_B\) (the reference point, e.g. a pin on a driven crank)✓ \(\omega r\)✓ ⟂ crank
\(\vec v_{C/B}\)? (it holds \(\omega_{BC}\))✓ ⟂ BC
\(\vec v_C\) (the point you want)?✓ along guide or ⟂ its crank

Two question marks, both of them sizes. That is the standard situation, and it means the diagram is a triangle with one fully known side and two known directions.

The recipe: drawing a relative velocity diagram

  1. Draw the mechanism neatly, roughly to scale, and label every pin. Mark the angles you will need.Every direction in the velocity diagram is copied from this drawing. A sloppy sketch gives sloppy perpendiculars.
  2. Find the bar lengths and angles from the dimensions (Pythagoras and \(\tan^{-1}\)).You need each bar’s angle to draw its perpendicular, and its length to turn \(v_{\text{rel}}\) into \(\omega\).
  3. Write the equation with the unknown point on the left: \(\vec v_{\text{unknown}} = \vec v_{\text{known}} + \vec v_{\text{unknown}/\text{known}}\).Then every term on the right starts from something you know, which fixes the order of drawing.
  4. Fill in the audit table, size and direction for each term. Calculate any known sizes now, such as \(v_B = \omega_{AB} r_{AB}\).
  5. Choose a scale so that the biggest vector is 8–15 cm long, and write it on the page (for example, “1 m/s = 20 mm”).Bigger diagrams give more accurate readings, and the memo awards a mark for using the given scale.
  6. Mark an origin o and draw the fully known vector from it, with an arrowhead and a label.
  7. Through the tip of that vector, draw a long, thin line perpendicular to the bar. This is the direction of \(\vec v_{\text{rel}}\). You do not know where it ends yet, so do not put an arrowhead on it.
  8. Through o, draw a long, thin line in the direction the unknown point must move (along its guide, or perpendicular to its crank).The unknown absolute velocity also starts at o, because every absolute velocity is measured from the same fixed ground.
  9. The two lines cross at the tip of the unknown velocity. Now draw both arrows: the absolute one from o to the crossing, and the relative one from the tip of the known vector to the crossing. Label everything.
  10. Measure and convert with your scale (or solve the triangle with the sine rule). Then \(\omega_{\text{bar}} = v_{\text{rel}}/r_{\text{bar}}\), and find its sense with the rule below.

Clockwise or anticlockwise? Read it off the diagram

The pin-and-push rule

\(\vec v_{C/B}\) is how C moves as seen from B. So put your finger on the mechanism at B (the letter after the slash) and hold it still. Push the other end, C, in the direction of the \(\vec v_{C/B}\) arrow from your diagram. Whichever way the bar turns, that is the sense of \(\omega_{BC}\).

The same rule works for a crank on a fixed pivot: hold the pivot and push the pin in the direction of its velocity. It also works in Chapter 10 for \(\alpha\), using the tangential arrow. If you swap the order (\(\vec v_{B/C}\) instead of \(\vec v_{C/B}\)), the arrow flips and the pinned point swaps, so you get the same answer either way.

Worked example 9.1: the sliding ladder

L14 Example 1

Roller A moves right at 3 m/s. Find the velocity of B and the angular velocity of the 1.5 m bar when \(\theta = 30^\circ\).

Equation: B is the unknown point, so \(\vec v_B = \vec v_A + \vec v_{B/A}\).

TermSizeDirection
\(\vec v_A\)✓ 3 m/s✓ → (floor)
\(\vec v_{B/A}\)? \(= 1.5\,\omega\)✓ ⟂ AB
\(\vec v_B\)?✓ vertical (wall)
  1. The triangle has a right angle at o and 30° at the bottom, so \(v_B = \frac{v_A}{\tan30^\circ} = 5.20\) m/s and \(v_{B/A} = \frac{v_A}{\sin30^\circ} = 6.00\) m/s.
  2. \(\omega = v_{B/A}/r_{AB} = 6.00/1.5 = 4.00\) rad/s.
  3. Sense: pin A, and push B along \(\vec v_{B/A}\), which points down and to the left. B sits up and to the left of A, so pushing it down-left swings the bar anticlockwise.This is the pin-and-push rule. It agrees with the instantaneous centre in Chapter 8.

vB = 5.20 m/s ↓, ωAB = 4.00 rad/s CCW

Check by vector algebra (L14, “vector solution”)

Write every vector in components and equate. With \(\vec r_{B/A} = -1.299\hat i + 0.75\hat j\):

\[ -v_B\hat j = 3\hat i + \omega\hat k\times(-1.299\hat i + 0.75\hat j) = (3 - 0.75\omega)\hat i - 1.299\omega\,\hat j \]

The \(\hat i\) parts give \(0 = 3 - 0.75\omega\), so \(\omega = 4\) (positive means CCW). The \(\hat j\) parts give \(v_B = 1.299(4) = 5.20\). This is the same equation as the diagram, in a different language. It is a good check when you have time.

Worked example 9.2: the slider-crank engine

L15 Example 2 (also the start of L16 Example 2)

Crank OB (125 mm) turns clockwise at 1500 rev/min. Connecting rod AB is 350 mm. Find the piston velocity \(v_A\) and \(\omega_{AB}\) when \(\theta = 60^\circ\).

  1. Known pin: \(\omega_{OB} = 1500\times\frac{2\pi}{60} = 157.1\) rad/s, so \(v_B = 157.1\times0.125 = 19.6\) m/s, perpendicular to OB. For a clockwise crank with B up and to the left of O, that points up and to the right at 30°.
  2. Rod angle: B is \(0.125\sin60^\circ = 0.108\) m above the slider line, so \(\sin\beta = 0.108/0.350\) and \(\beta = 18.0^\circ\).You need β to draw the perpendicular to AB in the diagram.
  3. Equation, with A unknown: \(\vec v_A = \vec v_B + \vec v_{A/B}\). \(\vec v_B\) is fully known, \(\vec v_{A/B}\) is ⟂ AB with size unknown, and \(\vec v_A\) is horizontal with size unknown.
  1. Sine rule (each side over the sine of the angle opposite it): \(\frac{v_A}{\sin78^\circ} = \frac{v_B}{\sin72^\circ} = \frac{v_{A/B}}{\sin30^\circ}\). This gives \(v_A = 20.2\) m/s and \(v_{A/B} = 10.3\) m/s.All three directions are known, so all three angles are known. That is exactly when the sine rule is the right tool.
  2. \(\omega_{AB} = 10.3/0.350 = 29.5\) rad/s. Pin B and push A along \(\vec v_{A/B}\) (down, slightly right). A is the left end, so the bar turns anticlockwise.

vA = 20.2 m/s →, ωAB = 29.5 rad/s CCW

Worked example 9.3: three bars, from a past exam

2016 exam (a)–(b), L17 slides

Bar AB turns clockwise at a constant 10 rad/s. Draw the relative velocity diagram of bar BD and find the angular velocities of BD and DE.

  1. Geometry: \(r_{BD} = \sqrt{0.25^2 + 0.6^2} = 0.65\) m, and BD rises at \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.25/0.6) = 22.6^\circ\).
  2. Known pin: \(v_B = \omega_{AB}\,r_{AB} = 10(0.2) = 2.00\) m/s. AB is vertical with B below A, so for clockwise rotation B moves left.Pin A and turn the bar clockwise: the bottom end swings to the left.
  3. D is on DE, which pivots at E. DE is horizontal, so \(\vec v_D\) is vertical (perpendicular to DE).
  4. Equation: \(\vec v_D = \vec v_B + \vec v_{D/B}\). \(\vec v_B\) is known completely, \(\vec v_{D/B}\) is ⟂ BD (size ?), and \(\vec v_D\) is vertical (size ?). That is two unknowns, so the triangle will close.
  1. \(v_D = \frac{v_B}{\tan22.6^\circ} = 4.80\) m/s ↓ and \(v_{D/B} = \frac{v_B}{\sin22.6^\circ} = 5.20\) m/s.
  2. \(\omega_{BD} = 5.20/0.65 = 8.00\) rad/s. Pin B and push D (down and left of B) towards the lower right: anticlockwise.
  3. \(\omega_{DE} = v_D/r_{DE} = 4.80/0.2 = 24.0\) rad/s. Pin E and push D (to the left of E) downwards: anticlockwise.

ωBD = 8.00 rad/s CCW, ωDE = 24.0 rad/s CCW (as in the memo)

Same triangle, different-looking memo

The memo writes \(\vec v_B = \vec v_D + \vec v_{B/D}\) instead. That is the same equation rearranged: \(\vec v_{B/D} = -\vec v_{D/B}\), so the relative arrow points the other way along the same side of the triangle. Both are marked correct. Pick one form and keep the arrows consistent with it.

Worked example 9.4: a slider on a slope, from a past exam

Final exam 2022 Q4(a), Review lecture 1

Bar AB has \(\omega_{AB} = 3\) rad/s CCW at this instant. Block C slides on a 3-4-5 incline. Find the angular velocity of bar BC.

  1. Known pin: \(v_B = 3(0.07) = 0.21\) m/s. B is above A and the rotation is anticlockwise, so B moves left.
  2. Angles: BC makes \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(50/120) = 22.6^\circ\) with the vertical. The slope is at \(\beta = \tan^{-1}(3/4) = 36.9^\circ\) to the horizontal.
  3. Equation: \(\vec v_C = \vec v_B + \vec v_{C/B}\), with \(\vec v_C\) along the slope (size ?) and \(\vec v_{C/B}\) ⟂ BC, which is 22.6° below horizontal (size ?).
  1. Sine rule: \(\frac{v_{C/B}}{\sin36.9^\circ} = \frac{v_B}{\sin120.5^\circ}\), so \(v_{C/B} = 0.146\) m/s.
  2. \(\omega_{BC} = 0.146/0.13 = 1.125\) rad/s. Pin B and push C (below-left of B) towards the lower right: anticlockwise.

ωBC = 1.125 rad/s CCW (memo: 1.125 rad/s CCW)

The memo gives a tick for each of: \(v_B\) with its direction, the length CB, each of the two angles, the equation, the vector diagram, the arrows, and the final answer with its sense. It is the full recipe above, written down.

A special case: when the diagram collapses

Worked example 9.5: the bar that is not rotating

Final exam 2021 Q5(a), Review lecture 2

Arm AB turns clockwise at a constant 6 rad/s. Find the angular velocity of bar BDE at the instant shown.

  1. \(v_B = 6(0.09) = 0.54\) m/s. B is above A and the rotation is clockwise, so B moves to the right.
  2. D is on the vertical arm CD, so \(\vec v_D\) is horizontal.
  3. Equation \(\vec v_D = \vec v_B + \vec v_{D/B}\): \(\vec v_{D/B}\) must be ⟂ BD, which is tilted, while \(\vec v_D\) and \(\vec v_B\) are both horizontal.
  1. \(v_{D/B} = 0\), so \(\omega_{BDE} = 0\). At this instant BDE is translating, and every point on it moves at 0.54 m/s to the right.The perpendiculars to \(\vec v_B\) and \(\vec v_D\) are two parallel vertical lines that never meet, so the instantaneous centre is at infinity (Chapter 8).
  2. \(v_D = 0.54\) m/s, so \(\omega_{DC} = 0.54/0.18 = 3.00\) rad/s clockwise.

ωBDE = 0 (instantaneous translation), ωDC = 3.00 rad/s CW

Zero angular velocity does not mean zero angular acceleration. In Chapter 10 this same bar has \(\alpha = 7.2\) rad/s².

Common slips with velocity diagrams
  • Drawing \(\vec v_{\text{rel}}\) along the bar instead of perpendicular to it. The bar cannot stretch, so there is never a component along it.
  • Starting the unknown absolute velocity from the tip of a vector instead of from o. Absolute velocities all start at o.
  • Using the wrong length in \(\omega = v_{\text{rel}}/r\). Use the distance between the two points in the equation.
  • Forgetting to state the sense (CW or CCW) of each \(\omega\). It is a separate mark.
  • Not converting rev/min to rad/s.
In one breath
  • \(\vec v_C = \vec v_B + \vec v_{C/B}\), with \(\vec v_{C/B}\) ⟂ BC and of size \(\omega_{BC}\,r_{BC}\).
  • Audit first: at most two unknowns, usually two sizes.
  • Known vector from o. Perpendicular line through its tip. Direction line for the unknown point through o. Close at the crossing.
  • \(\omega = v_{\text{rel}}/r\). Sense by pin-and-push.
  • Practice: Tut04 Q1–Q4 (answers are on the sheet), and redo Tut04 with this method as the Relative Velocity page suggests.
Chapter 10 · Lectures L16–L17 · the heart of the book, part 2

Relative acceleration: drawing the acceleration diagram

In this chapter
  • Why the relative acceleration has two parts, and which part is always known
  • The accelerations of pins, sliders and rolling wheels
  • The “two chains” recipe for an acceleration diagram that always closes
  • Worked examples: ladder, engine, and the 2016, 2021 and 2022 exam questions
  • Rolling without slipping, and a slider-crank you can turn by hand

The equation, and why it has two relative parts

Differentiate \(\vec v_B = \vec v_A + \vec v_{B/A}\) and you get \(\vec a_B = \vec a_A + \vec a_{B/A}\). Chapter 9 showed that, seen from A, point B moves on a circle of radius \(r_{AB}\). Chapter 3 showed that motion on a circle has two acceleration components. Put those together:

\[ \vec a_B = \vec a_A + (\vec a_{B/A})_n + (\vec a_{B/A})_t \qquad \begin{cases} (a_{B/A})_n = \omega^2 r_{AB} & \text{from B towards A} \\[2pt] (a_{B/A})_t = \alpha\, r_{AB} & \perp AB \end{cases} \]
Why the normal part is always known (and why velocities come first)

The normal part \(\omega^2 r\) depends only on \(\omega\) (from the velocity diagram) and the bar length, and it always points along the bar towards the reference point. So once the velocity diagram is solved, every normal component in the problem is fully known: size and direction. That is why the exam always asks for the velocity diagram first, and why the amber arrows in this book are always drawn before the green ones.

The tangential part \(\alpha r\) is perpendicular to the bar (direction known) but its size contains the unknown \(\alpha\). It plays exactly the role that \(\vec v_{B/A}\) played in Chapter 9.

In vector form (L16): \(\vec a_B = \vec a_A - \omega^2\vec r_{B/A} + \vec\alpha\times\vec r_{B/A}\). The \(\omega^2\) term is not a cross product. It is \(\omega^2\) times \(\vec r_{B/A}\), with a minus sign, which is just the arrow from B back towards A.

Accelerations of the usual suspects

PointNormal partTangential part
Pin on a crank about a fixed pivot\(\omega^2 r\), towards the pivot (known once \(\omega\) is known)\(\alpha r\), ⟂ crank. Zero if \(\omega\) is constant. Unknown if \(\alpha\) is what you want.
Slider in a straight guideOnly one part, along the guide. Size usually unknown. (A straight path has no normal acceleration.)
Centre of a wheel rolling without slip\(a_O = \alpha r\), parallel to the surface
Contact point of a rolling wheel\(\omega^2 r\) towards the wheel’s centre. Not zero! (Chapter 8’s trap.)
Gear teeth in contactDifferent for each gearEqual: \(\alpha_1 r_1 = \alpha_2 r_2\)

The recipe: two chains that meet

An acceleration diagram has more arrows than a velocity diagram, but there are still only two unknowns. The trick is to organise the equation so that each unknown comes last in a chain of arrows that starts at o.

\[ \underbrace{(\vec a_C)_n + (\vec a_C)_t}_{\text{chain 1: what C does on its own path}} \;=\; \underbrace{\vec a_B + (\vec a_{C/B})_n + (\vec a_{C/B})_t}_{\text{chain 2: reach C via B}} \]
  1. Solve the velocity diagram first. Write down every \(\omega\) with its sense.Every \(\omega^2 r\) term needs these.
  2. Write the equation with the unknown point on the left, splitting every acceleration on a curved path into \(n\) and \(t\). This is the form the memos tick:
    \[ (\vec a_C)_n + (\vec a_C)_t = (\vec a_B)_n + (\vec a_B)_t + (\vec a_{C/B})_n + (\vec a_{C/B})_t \]
  3. Audit table: size and direction of every term. Calculate all the normal parts now. Expect exactly two question marks, both of them sizes of perpendicular terms (or of a slider’s acceleration).
  4. Choose and state a scale, for example 1 mm = 2 m/s².
  5. Chain 2 first: from o, draw the known parts of \(\vec a_B\) head to tail, then \((\vec a_{C/B})_n\) from its tip, pointing from C towards B.You can only draw a vector with an arrowhead when you know both its size and direction, so all the fully known vectors go down first.
  6. Through the end of chain 2, draw a long line perpendicular to BC, the direction of \((\vec a_{C/B})_t\).
  7. Chain 1: from o, draw the known part of C’s own acceleration. For a pin on a crank that is \((\vec a_C)_n\), towards that crank’s pivot. For a slider there is no known part, so start at o itself.
  8. Through the end of chain 1, draw a long line in the unknown direction: ⟂ the crank for \((\vec a_C)_t\), or along the guide for a slider.
  9. The two lines cross at the tip of \(\vec a_C\). Put arrowheads on both unknown vectors, finishing at the crossing.Both chains describe the same \(\vec a_C\), so they must end at the same point. The crossing is the only point that lies on both lines.
  10. Measure the two unknowns, convert with the scale, and get \(\alpha = (a_{\text{rel}})_t / r\). Find the sense with pin-and-push on the green arrow. Measure \(\vec a_C\) itself (o to the crossing) if it is asked for.
Normal points to the pin you measure from

\((\vec a_{C/B})_n\) points from C towards B, the letter after the slash. For a crank about a fixed pivot P, \((\vec a_C)_n\) points from C towards P. Every normal acceleration points inwards, towards the centre the point is circling (relative to that reference point).

Worked example 10.1: the ladder, first acceleration diagram

Continues worked example 9.1

The same ladder, with A moving right at a constant 3 m/s (so \(\vec a_A = 0\)). Find \(\vec a_B\) and \(\alpha_{AB}\) at \(\theta = 30^\circ\).

  1. From Chapter 9: \(\omega_{AB} = 4.00\) rad/s CCW.
  2. \((a_{B/A})_n = \omega^2 r = 4^2(1.5) = 24.0\) m/s², pointing from B towards A, so down and to the right along the bar.
  3. Equation: \(\vec a_B = \underbrace{\vec a_A}_{0} + (\vec a_{B/A})_n + (\vec a_{B/A})_t\). The unknowns are the size of \(\vec a_B\) (direction vertical) and the size of \((\vec a_{B/A})_t\) (direction ⟂ AB).
  1. Measured, or from components: \(a_B = 48.0\) m/s² and \((a_{B/A})_t = 41.6\) m/s².
  2. \(\alpha = 41.6/1.5 = 27.7\) rad/s². The green arrow points down-left at B. Pin A and push B that way: anticlockwise.

aB = 48.0 m/s² ↓, αAB = 27.7 rad/s² CCW

α has the same sense as ω, so the ladder’s rotation is speeding up as it falls flatter, which matches what you see when a ladder slips.

Worked example 10.2: the engine’s piston acceleration

L16 Example 2 (continues worked example 9.2)

Same slider-crank: crank 125 mm at a constant 1500 rev/min CW, rod 350 mm, \(\theta = 60^\circ\). Find \(\vec a_A\) and \(\alpha_{AB}\).

  1. From the velocity diagram: \(\omega_{OB} = 157.1\) rad/s CW and \(\omega_{AB} = 29.5\) rad/s CCW.
  2. B is on a crank with constant speed, so \((a_B)_t = 0\) and \(a_B = (a_B)_n = 157.1^2(0.125) = 3084\) m/s², from B towards O.
  3. \((a_{A/B})_n = \omega_{AB}^2\, r_{AB} = 29.5^2(0.350) = 305\) m/s², from A towards B (up the rod at 18°).The L16 slide prints 0.250 m here, but 305 only comes out with the real rod length, 0.350 m. That is a typo on the slide; the answer 305 is right.
  4. Unknowns: the size of \(\vec a_A\) (horizontal) and the size of \((\vec a_{A/B})_t\) (⟂ AB).
  1. Component check. The \(y\)-equation contains only one unknown, because \(\vec a_A\) is horizontal:
    \[ y:\ 0 = -3084\sin60^\circ + 305\sin18^\circ + 0.951\,(a_{A/B})_t \;\Rightarrow\; (a_{A/B})_t = 2710\ \text{m/s}^2 \]\[ x:\ a_A = 1542 + 290 - 0.309(2710) = 994\ \text{m/s}^2 \]
    Picking the equation in which one unknown has no component is the fastest way to solve these by hand.
  2. \(\alpha_{AB} = 2710/0.350 = 7740\) rad/s². The green arrow points up-left at A. Pin B and push A (the left end) upwards: clockwise.

aA = 994 m/s² →, αAB = 7740 rad/s² CW

Worked example 10.3: the 2016 exam, parts (c) and (d)

Continues worked example 9.3 · exam scale 1 mm = 2 m/s²

Draw the relative acceleration diagram of bar BD and use it to find \(\alpha_{BD}\). (AB turns at a constant 10 rad/s CW.)

From the velocity diagram: \(\omega_{BD} = 8.00\) rad/s CCW and \(\omega_{DE} = 24.0\) rad/s CCW. D is the point whose acceleration is not fully known, so put it on the left:

\[ (\vec a_D)_n + (\vec a_D)_t \;=\; \vec a_B + (\vec a_{D/B})_n + (\vec a_{D/B})_t \]
TermSizeDirection
\((\vec a_D)_n = \omega_{DE}^2 r_{DE}\)✓ \(24^2(0.2) = 115.2\)✓ D → E (→)
\((\vec a_D)_t = \alpha_{DE} r_{DE}\)?✓ ⟂ DE (vertical)
\(\vec a_B = \omega_{AB}^2 r_{AB}\) (and \((a_B)_t = 0\))✓ \(10^2(0.2) = 20.0\)✓ B → A (↑)
\((\vec a_{D/B})_n = \omega_{BD}^2 r_{BD}\)✓ \(8^2(0.65) = 41.6\)✓ D → B (22.6° above →)
\((\vec a_{D/B})_t = \alpha_{BD} r_{BD}\)?✓ ⟂ BD
  1. Measured: \((a_{D/B})_t \approx 200\) m/s². (Check: the \(x\)-components give \(115.2 = 0 + 38.4 + 0.385\,(a_{D/B})_t\), so it is 199.7.)
  2. \(\alpha_{BD} = 200/0.65 = 307\) rad/s². The green arrow points down-right. Pin B and push D (down-left of B) that way: anticlockwise.
  3. Bonus: \((a_D)_t = 148\) m/s² ↓, so \(\alpha_{DE} = 148/0.2 = 742\) rad/s² CCW.

αBD = 307 rad/s² CCW (memo: 307 rad/s² CCW)

Worked example 10.4: the 2022 exam, parts (b) and (c)

Continues worked example 9.4 · exam scale 1 m/s² : 20 cm

With \(\omega_{AB} = 3\) rad/s and \(\alpha_{AB} = 2\) rad/s², both CCW, draw the acceleration diagram for bar BC and find the acceleration of block C.

From the velocity diagram: \(\omega_{BC} = 1.125\) rad/s CCW. The new feature is that AB is speeding up, so B has a tangential part as well.

\[ \vec a_C \;=\; (\vec a_B)_n + (\vec a_B)_t + (\vec a_{C/B})_n + (\vec a_{C/B})_t \]
TermSize (m/s²)Direction
\((\vec a_B)_n = \omega_{AB}^2 r_{AB}\)✓ \(9(0.07) = 0.63\)✓ B → A (↓)
\((\vec a_B)_t = \alpha_{AB} r_{AB}\)✓ \(2(0.07) = 0.14\)✓ ⟂ AB, ← (pin A, spin CCW)
\((\vec a_{C/B})_n = \omega_{BC}^2 r_{BC}\)✓ \(1.125^2(0.13) = 0.1645\)✓ C → B (22.6° from vertical)
\((\vec a_{C/B})_t = \alpha_{BC} r_{BC}\)?✓ ⟂ BC (22.6° from horizontal)
\(\vec a_C\)?✓ along the slope (36.9°)
  1. Measure \(\vec a_C\) from o to the crossing: 0.547 m/s² (10.9 cm at 20 cm per m/s²). The memo accepts anything between 0.492 and 0.602 m/s², so neat drawing within 5% gets full marks.
  2. The green arrow is 0.39 m/s², so \(\alpha_{BC} = 0.39/0.13 = 3.0\) rad/s². Pin B and push C up-left: clockwise. (This part was not asked, but it is a useful check.)

aC = 0.547 m/s², directed down the slope

The mark people lose here

Because AB has an angular acceleration, \((\vec a_B)_t = \alpha_{AB} r_{AB}\) is not zero. The memo gives it its own tick “(mag. & dir.)”. Always ask whether the driving crank’s \(\omega\) is constant. If it is not, B has a tangential part.

Worked example 10.5: the 2021 exam, a bar with ω = 0

Final exam 2021 Q5(b)–(c) · continues worked example 9.5

AB turns at a constant 6 rad/s CW. Draw the relative acceleration diagram of BDE, find \(\alpha_{BDE}\), then find the acceleration of E.

  1. From the velocity diagram: \(\omega_{BDE} = 0\) and \(\omega_{DC} = 3.00\) rad/s CW.
  2. Equation for D:
    \[ (\vec a_D)_n + (\vec a_D)_t = (\vec a_B)_n + (\vec a_B)_t + (\vec a_{D/B})_n + (\vec a_{D/B})_t \]
  3. Terms: \((a_D)_n = 3^2(0.18) = 1.62\) ↓ (towards C). \((a_D)_t\): horizontal, size ?. \((a_B)_n = 6^2(0.09) = 3.24\) ↓ (towards A). \((a_B)_t = 0\) (constant ω). \((a_{D/B})_n = 0^2(0.242) = 0\). \((a_{D/B})_t\): ⟂ BD, size ?.With \(\omega_{BDE} = 0\), the normal relative term vanishes. This is the one situation where it does.
  1. The vertical components give \(-1.62 = -3.24 + (a_{D/B})_t\cos21.8^\circ\), so \((a_{D/B})_t = 1.745\) m/s².
  2. \(\alpha_{BDE} = 1.745/0.242 = 7.21\) rad/s². The green arrow points up-left at D. Pin B and push D (up-right of B) that way: anticlockwise.
  3. Part (c): E is on the same bar, so \(\vec a_E = \vec a_B + (\vec a_{E/B})_n + (\vec a_{E/B})_t\), with \((a_{E/B})_n = 0\) and \((a_{E/B})_t = 7.21(0.485) = 3.49\) m/s² ⟂ BE. In components:
    \[ \vec a_E = (0, -3.24) + 3.49(-0.371,\ 0.928) = (-1.30,\ 0)\ \text{m/s}^2 \]
    Once you know \(\alpha\) for a bar, any other point on it follows from one more relative acceleration equation.

αBDE = 7.2 rad/s² CCW, aE = 1.30 m/s² ← (memo: 7.2 rad/s² and 1.3 m/s² ←)

Rolling without slipping, and gears

For a wheel of radius \(r\) rolling on a fixed surface (L17):

\[ v_O = \omega r \qquad a_O = \alpha r \ (\text{parallel to the surface}) \qquad a_{\text{contact}} = \omega^2 r \ (\text{towards }O) \]
Why the contact point accelerates

The contact point is at rest for an instant, but a moment earlier it was coming down and a moment later it is lifting off. Its path is a cusp of a cycloid, and that sharp change of direction needs an acceleration of \(\omega^2 r\) straight up into the wheel. This is why you can never use the IC for accelerations.

Worked example 10.6: a gear rolling on a rack

L17 Example 1

A gear of radius 0.3 m rolls to the right on a fixed rack with \(\omega = 12\) rad/s and \(\alpha = 6\) rad/s², both clockwise. Find the acceleration of point A at the top.

  1. Use the centre O as the reference point, because its acceleration is known: \(a_O = \alpha r = 6(0.3) = 1.8\) m/s² →.
  2. \((a_{A/O})_n = \omega^2 r = 144(0.3) = 43.2\) m/s², from A towards O (↓). \((a_{A/O})_t = \alpha r = 1.8\) m/s², ⟂ OA. For CW α at the top of the wheel that is →.
  3. Add head to tail: \(\vec a_A = (1.8 + 1.8)\hat i - 43.2\hat j\).

aA = 43.3 m/s² at ∡ −85.2°

Two gears in mesh share the same \(a_t\) at the contact point (\(\alpha_1 r_1 = \alpha_2 r_2\)), but each has its own \(a_n = \omega^2 r\), so their total accelerations at the contact differ (L17, “bodies in contact”).

Lab: turn the crank yourself

Drag the slider to change the crank angle of the engine from worked examples 9.2 and 10.2. Watch how the two diagrams change shape. Things to look for: at 0° and 180° (dead centres), the piston’s velocity is zero but its acceleration is at its largest. And the green arrow flips direction as the rod’s angular acceleration changes sense.

Mechanism

Velocity diagram

Acceleration diagram

Each diagram is rescaled to fit its box, so compare shapes, not lengths, between angles. Crank 125 mm, rod 350 mm, 1500 rev/min CW.

Common slips with acceleration diagrams
  • Starting on accelerations before the velocities are solved. Every normal term needs an \(\omega\).
  • Pointing a normal arrow the wrong way. It always points towards the reference point or the pivot.
  • Forgetting \((a_B)_t\) when the driving crank has an \(\alpha\), or putting one in when \(\omega\) is constant.
  • Drawing the tangential term along the bar. It is always ⟂ to the bar, like the relative velocity.
  • Squaring the wrong thing: it is \(\omega^2 r\), not \((\omega r)^2\).
  • Using the IC to find accelerations.
  • Not stating the sense of \(\alpha\) (CW/CCW). It is a separate mark.
In one breath
  • \(\vec a_C = \vec a_B + (\vec a_{C/B})_n + (\vec a_{C/B})_t\). The normal part is \(\omega^2 r\) towards B (known after the velocities). The tangential part is \(\alpha r\), ⟂ BC (direction only).
  • Points on cranks have \(n\) and \(t\) parts. Sliders have one part, along the guide.
  • Two chains from o, unknowns last. Their direction lines cross at the answer.
  • \(\alpha = (a_{\text{rel}})_t/r\). Sense by pin-and-push on the green arrow.
  • Practice: Tut05 Q1–Q5 (answers on the sheet).
Chapter 11 · Revision

Exam playbook and one-page formula sheet

The diagram question checklist

This list is built from the 2016, 2021 and 2022 memos. Each line matches something the markers tick.

  1. Geometry first. Bar lengths (Pythagoras) and angles (\(\tan^{-1}\)). Write them down: they are marks.
  2. Driving crank: \(v = \omega r\), with direction and a sketch arrow. Convert rev/min to rad/s.
  3. Velocity equation written out, e.g. \(\vec v_C = \vec v_B + \vec v_{C/B}\).
  4. Audit: size and direction of each term, known or not.
  5. Velocity diagram to the given scale, with arrows on every vector, labels, and angles marked.
  6. \(\omega\) of each bar = relative velocity ÷ length, with sense (CW or CCW).
  7. Acceleration equation with every \(n\) and \(t\) part written separately.
  8. Audit: every normal part calculated (\(\omega^2 r\)) with its direction (“towards ___”). Every tangential part as “\(\alpha r\), ⟂ ___, ?”.
  9. Acceleration diagram to scale: known arrows first, two direction lines, crossing, arrowheads on everything.
  10. Measure, convert, then \(\alpha\) = tangential ÷ length, with sense. Answers within about ±5% earn full marks.

Choosing a scale when none is given

Find the largest known vector and aim for 10–15 cm. For example, 0.63 m/s² at 1 m/s² : 20 cm is 12.6 cm. 3084 m/s² at 1 mm = 25 m/s² is 123 mm. Always write the scale beside the diagram. Draw thin, sharp lines; use set squares for perpendiculars and a protractor for angles. Practise with the course app (convect.uct.ac.za) and then on paper, because the exam is on paper.

If you get stuck

  • Count the unknowns. More than two means you have missed a known direction (a slider’s guide, a crank’s perpendicular) or need another equation for a different bar.
  • Check the IC for a fast sanity check of any \(\omega\) (Chapter 8).
  • Switch to components (vector algebra) if the diagram looks wrong. Pick the component direction in which one unknown disappears.
  • Parallel velocities on a bar mean \(\omega = 0\) for that bar, so its normal relative term is zero, but not its \(\alpha\).

Formula sheet: Part I on one page

TopicFormulasRemember
Rectilinear\(v=\dot s,\ a=\dot v,\ a\,ds=v\,dv\)
Constant \(a\): \(v=v_0+at,\ s=s_0+v_0t+\frac12at^2,\ v^2=v_0^2+2a\Delta s\)		Ask what \(a\) depends on. Constant-\(a\) equations only if \(a\) is constant.
GraphsSlope of \(s\)–\(t\) = \(v\), slope of \(v\)–\(t\) = \(a\), area under \(v\)–\(t\) = \(\Delta s\), area under \(a\)–\(s\) = \(\frac12\Delta(v^2)\)Integrating raises the curve’s power by one.
Projectile\(a_x=0,\ a_y=-g\)Time links x and y.
n–t\(a_t=\dot v,\ a_n=v^2/\rho\)\(a_n\) points into the bend.
Polar\(v_r=\dot r,\ v_\theta=r\dot\theta\)
\(a_r=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2,\ a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta\)		List \(r,\dot r,\ddot r,\dot\theta,\ddot\theta\) first.
Relative (particles)\(\vec v_B=\vec v_A+\vec v_{B/A},\ \vec a_B=\vec a_A+\vec a_{B/A}\)Non-rotating observer. \(\vec v_{A/B}=-\vec v_{B/A}\).
Pulleys\(\sum (\text{segment lengths}) = \text{const}\) → differentiate. Centre speed = average of the side speeds.A pulley in a loop counts twice.
Fixed-axis rotation\(\omega=\dot\theta,\ \alpha=\dot\omega,\ \omega\,d\omega=\alpha\,d\theta\)
\(v=\omega r,\ a_n=\omega^2r,\ a_t=\alpha r\)		\(\omega\) [rad/s] = rev/min × 2π/60. Contacts share \(v\) and \(a_t\).
Rolling (no slip)\(v_O=\omega r,\ a_O=\alpha r,\ a_{\text{contact}}=\omega^2 r\) (towards O)Contact point: \(v=0\), \(a\neq0\).
IC\(v=\omega\cdot r_{\text{to IC}}\), ⟂ to the line to the ICVelocities only. Never accelerations.
Relative velocity (rigid)\(\vec v_B=\vec v_A+\vec\omega\times\vec r_{B/A}\), \(\ v_{B/A}=\omega r_{AB}\) ⟂ ABKnown vector from o; ⟂ line through its tip; direction line through o.
Relative acceleration (rigid)\(\vec a_B=\vec a_A-\omega^2\vec r_{B/A}+\vec\alpha\times\vec r_{B/A}\)
\((a_{B/A})_n=\omega^2r\) (B → A), \((a_{B/A})_t=\alpha r\) (⟂ AB)		Velocities first. Two chains from o, unknowns last.
The whole of Part I in four sentences

Velocity is the slope of position, and acceleration is the slope of velocity. On a curve, acceleration splits into a part that changes speed and a part, \(v^2/\rho\), that turns you into the bend. On a rigid body, any point’s motion is a reference point’s motion plus a spin about it, and that spin always moves the point perpendicular to the line joining them. Draw that as a triangle for velocities and a polygon for accelerations, and you can solve every mechanism in this course.

Written as a study companion for MEC2047S Dynamics I, built on the course's lecture notes L01–L17, tutorials 0–5 and the two review lectures. Every worked number was re-computed, and each velocity and acceleration diagram is drawn to scale from those computed values. Part II (kinetics: Newton's second law, energy, momentum and rigid-body kinetics) comes next.
